THE DIFF (three-dot, against merge-base):
    git diff main...HEAD -M
Commit list:
    git log main..HEAD --oneline
One commit: 56ab6b4 "refactor(#168): read the rules when a step needs them, not four files early".

THE SPEC — GitHub issue #168 on this repo. Fetch the full body yourself:
    gh issue view 168

Its acceptance criteria, quoted so you cannot miss them:
- [ ] No unit inlines a rule file it does not use on every run
- [ ] A unit needing a profile value names the value and where it comes from, without the whole file arriving first
- [ ] A fresh install with no `project-profile.md` produces a stated outcome rather than a dangling reference — under whichever rule (2) settles on
- [ ] #129's pruning is done against whatever the trim leaves actually reading the profile

CRITICAL CONTEXT — the issue explicitly splits into two halves:

> Two halves, and only the first is mechanical:
> 1. **The eager inlining.** Replace the preamble with a named reference each unit reads when it needs it. No doctrine changes — the same unit resolves the same values from the same file, just not four files early.
> 2. **The resolution rule.** Whether a unit *stops* when the profile is missing, as `profile-doctrine` says today, or degrades with stated defaults. #143 decided the stop deliberately and #150 extends it. Reversing that is a real decision, not cleanup, and it is the one that decides how the first ten minutes with this plugin feel.
>
> Recommendation: do (1) now, and decide (2) with a fresh install in front of you rather than in the abstract.

**The commit deliberately implements half 1 only.** Judge whether that deferral is legitimate per the issue's own recommendation, and whether half 1 is completely done — do NOT simply report half 2 as a missing requirement without addressing the issue's explicit recommendation to defer it. Also judge whether the third acceptance criterion ("a stated outcome … under whichever rule (2) settles on") can in fact be satisfied while (2) is unsettled, which is what the commit claims by stating today's stop rule.

Things to check concretely:
- Does any unit still inline a rule file? (The old form was lines beginning with `@`.)
- `profile-doctrine.md` was dropped entirely from all four units. Was it "used on every run"? Is dropping it in scope for half 1, or is it an unrequested removal?
- The `doc-gen-readme` and `doc-review-readme` units gained NEW inline profile citations (diagrams dir, README output path, audience) that did not exist before. Is that criterion 2 being satisfied, or scope creep beyond "replace the preamble"?
- Criterion 4 references #129 (already closed). Check whether every section `.claude/rules/project-profile.md` declares is still cited by some unit, and whether any unit cites a section that does not exist.
- The commit message claims half 2 is untouched. Verify no wording in the diff actually changes the stop-vs-degrade rule rather than merely restating it.

YOUR BRIEF:
Report: (a) requirements the spec asked for that are missing or partial; (b) behaviour in the diff that wasn't asked for (scope creep); (c) requirements that look implemented but where the implementation looks wrong. Quote the spec line for each finding.

**Under 400 words.** Your final message IS the report — no preamble, no offer to help further.

## What to build

Every command opens with the same preamble:

```
@${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/rules/<workflow>.md
@${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/rules/anti-slop.md          (some units)
@${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/rules/agent-report.md
@${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/rules/profile-doctrine.md
@.claude/rules/project-profile.md
```

Four files inlined on every invocation, whether that run needs them or not. The platform's guidance is the opposite — keep the unit short, name what it may need, let it be read when it is needed: *"Keep `SKILL.md` under 500 lines. Move detailed reference material to separate files."*

The last line is the adopter's problem specifically. `@.claude/rules/project-profile.md` points into **their** repo, at a file they have not written on the day they install the plugin. First run, first reference, nothing behind it.

Two halves, and only the first is mechanical:

1. **The eager inlining.** Replace the preamble with a named reference each unit reads when it needs it. No doctrine changes — the same unit resolves the same values from the same file, just not four files early.
2. **The resolution rule.** Whether a unit *stops* when the profile is missing, as `profile-doctrine` says today, or degrades with stated defaults. #143 decided the stop deliberately and #150 extends it. Reversing that is a real decision, not cleanup, and it is the one that decides how the first ten minutes with this plugin feel.

Recommendation: do (1) now, and decide (2) with a fresh install in front of you rather than in the abstract.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No unit inlines a rule file it does not use on every run
- [ ] A unit needing a profile value names the value and where it comes from, without the whole file arriving first
- [ ] A fresh install with no `project-profile.md` produces a stated outcome rather than a dangling reference — under whichever rule (2) settles on
- [ ] #129's pruning is done against whatever the trim leaves actually reading the profile

## Blocked by

None, but it wants the skill-form move landing beside it — both rewrite the head of every unit.

=== profile-doctrine.md ===
# profile-doctrine

Where the line falls between what every project shares and what belongs to one project.
This file is the same everywhere and is not edited downstream; the values it talks about
live in the project, at `.claude/rules/project-profile.md`.

## The profile

The shipped commands and skills state their *intent* and resolve any project-specific
value — a path, an ID scheme, a label, an integration, a format, an audience — **from the
project's profile**, instead of hardcoding it. Customize a workflow by editing that file,
not the units.

**How a unit uses it.** Where a command or skill would otherwise bake in a value, it
points at the matching section of the profile (e.g. "create the *plan* label — see
project-profile → Labels"). The values a project starts with are **defaults**: they
reproduce this toolkit's own behaviour, so a project that changes nothing behaves exactly
as the toolkit does. Adoption is opt-in — change a line in the profile and every unit
follows.

**Two wiring styles, and when each applies.** A unit that **inlines the profile** at the
top may then show a value inline as an illustrated default — the whole file is already in
front of it, and its group rule carries the "these resolve from the profile" statement for
the group, so the pointer is not repeated line by line. A unit that **does not inline it**
is read on its own, with nothing beside it, so it points at the profile at each point of
use. Both are correct. Which one applies is decided by whether the unit inlines the
profile — not by preference.

**No profile, no defaults.** A project that has not declared its values does not fall back
to another project's — a unit that needs a value it cannot resolve stops and says so. A
silent fallback would run one project's paths, labels, and ID scheme inside another, with
nothing in the session to reveal it.

**Where a stop is not available.** A unit sometimes needs a value only *after* something it
cannot undo — tidying up after a merge, say. Stopping there is not a stop; it is a report
in a stop's clothing. So a unit like that resolves the value at its **earliest** point
instead, raises whatever will not resolve at the human gate it already has, and then
proceeds and reports the gap. The promise above is unchanged in substance: the value still
never resolves silently, and nothing is ever guessed to fill the hole. What moves is only
*where* it is said — because refusing finished work over a missing key protects nobody, and
a gap named after the fact is news rather than a decision.

## Two halves, two citation forms

A unit reaches each half by a different path, so the two carry the distinction themselves
and there is no resolution order to remember.

| Cited as | Means | Lives |
|---|---|---|
| `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/rules/…` | doctrine — identical everywhere | the plugin, travelling with the units |
| `.claude/rules/project-profile.md` | values — this project's | the project, one file per repo |

A unit that inlines them does so at the top with `@`; one that does not reads them by path
at the point of use. In a project that has declared nothing, the values reference resolves
to nothing and the session shows it — the no-fallback rule above, enforced by mechanism
rather than by prose.

## What belongs in the profile, and what does not

The profile is for **declarative** customization — a value or a list. A whole
**procedure** (e.g. how to publish to Confluence and review the render) is *not* a value;
it belongs in its own project-owned skill, never crammed into a general unit. Lists → the
profile; procedures → a project skill. This is the rules files' "what this owns vs. what
it hands off" boundary, made concrete.

The same line binds the **units**. A value the profile can restate is safe for a unit to
show inline; a *procedure* never is — how drift is detected, how files are laid out. No
value can override a procedure, so a project that does it another way is forced to edit a
shipped unit, and its repo then reads as drifted when it was only working around us. State
the goal; let the profile or the project's own layer name the mechanism.

## More than one plugin writes this file

A project may place several plugins that all resolve against the same
`project-profile.md`. Each reads a different set of sections, so a **setup unit writes only
the sections its own plugin reads** — never the whole file.

That makes the write order irrelevant, which is the whole point. A project runs one
plugin's setup today and another's next month, and must end with both plugins' values
intact; neither setup can know which ran first, so neither may assume it is the only
author.

- **Own only what you read.** A section a plugin does not resolve against is not its
  business — not to write, not to reformat, not to remove. A section **no** plugin claims
  is the project's own, and is never touched.
- **Add or update in place; never truncate.** A setup unit that finds an existing profile
  edits the sections it owns and leaves the rest exactly as it found them. Writing the file
  out from a template is what loses another plugin's values, and it does it silently.
- **A value already there is a decision.** This file exists to be hand-edited, so a setup
  unit re-running over one does not overwrite what it finds. It shows what differs from its
  defaults and asks. Only a section that is *absent* gets written without asking.

The **doctrine half** — the preamble saying what a profile is — is written by whichever
setup unit first finds it missing. It is identical in every project, so the next one to run
finds it already correct and leaves it alone.

## Where a project's own units live

A project may have commands and skills of its own — ones no other project wants. They stay
in the project, and they take a `<repo-name>-` prefix, so a project's unit can never be
mistaken for, or collide with, one every project shares.

Project-specific **rules** take no prefix. A rule is reached by path from the unit citing
it, so it has no namespace to collide in, and `paths:` front-matter already scopes it to
the files it governs. `workflow-patterns.md` scoped to `.github/workflows/**` is correctly
named; `myrepo-workflow-patterns.md` would only be noise.

# Generate a README

## Rules

Read each one when the step that needs it arrives, not before:

- `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/rules/doc-workflow.md` — where this sits in the pipeline and
  what it hands to the gate rather than doing itself
- `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/rules/anti-slop.md` — the standard `doc-review-readme` will
  judge this output against, worth reading before Step 5 rather than after
- `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/rules/agent-report.md` — what the Step 6 hand-off owes its reader
- `.claude/rules/project-profile.md` — **this project's values.** Every
  "see project-profile → X" below means that file, section X

**No profile, no run.** If that last file is absent the project has not adopted this
plugin. Stop at the first value you cannot resolve — the README's output path and the
diagram policy both come from it — and say which one it was; `setup-agent-workflows`
writes the file.

Research best practices, study the project, and write its README — diagrams and all.

Target: $ARGUMENTS  (a repo path, or empty for the current repo)

## PURPOSE
